labels.name: how_collaboration
labels.description: How this person collaborates with others, teamwork style
examples: Prefers pair programming for complex features
Likes async code reviews over synchronous walkthroughs
Thrives in small cross-functional teams (3-5 people)
Prefers to work independently and sync at standups
labels.classification_guidance: Captures the person's teamwork and collaboration patterns, including whether they prefer pair programming, async collaboration, or in-person brainstorming. Distinct from communication style which focuses on channels and tone rather than group dynamics.
anti_examples: Prefers Slack over email → use how_communication

labels.name: how_communication
labels.description: How they communicate — channels, frequency, style preferences
examples: Prefers Slack for quick questions, email for formal requests
Likes async communication over real-time meetings
Prefers video calls with camera on for team meetings
Sends detailed written updates instead of holding meetings
labels.classification_guidance: Covers preferred communication channels (Slack, email, video calls), frequency of check-ins, and interaction patterns. Focuses on the mechanics of communication rather than personality-driven tone (see who_communication_style).
anti_examples: Is direct and blunt → use who_communication_style

labels.name: how_content_creation
labels.description: How they create content — writing, video, design approaches
examples: Writes blog posts in Markdown, publishes on personal site
Creates technical videos with screen recordings and voiceover
Designs in Figma, follows a mobile-first approach
Outlines extensively before writing — never writes ad-hoc
labels.classification_guidance: Describes their approach to creating content such as blog posts, videos, documentation, or design artifacts. Includes tools, processes, and creative methodology.
anti_examples: Published a paper on ML → use what_publications_ip

labels.name: how_decision_making
labels.description: How they make decisions — analytical, intuitive, collaborative
examples: Highly data-driven, needs metrics before deciding
Trusts gut instinct for people decisions, data for tech decisions
Prefers to get input from the team before committing
Conservative with risk — prefers proven approaches
labels.classification_guidance: Captures decision-making methodology: data-driven vs intuitive, consensus-seeking vs autonomous, risk-tolerant vs conservative. Describes the process, not the outcomes.
anti_examples: Prioritizes family over work → use why_priorities

labels.name: how_learning
labels.description: How they learn — visual, hands-on, reading, courses, mentorship
examples: Learns best by building projects from scratch
Prefers video tutorials over written docs
Reads research papers and technical books
Benefits from pair programming with more experienced devs
labels.classification_guidance: Describes learning modalities and preferences: video tutorials, reading documentation, hands-on experimentation, formal courses, or mentorship. Focuses on the process of acquiring knowledge, not what they know.
anti_examples: Has a CS degree → use what_education

labels.name: how_problem_solving
labels.description: How they approach and solve problems
examples: Breaks problems down into small, testable hypotheses
Likes to whiteboard and diagram before coding
Uses rubber-duck debugging regularly
Starts with the simplest possible solution, then iterates
labels.classification_guidance: Captures problem-solving approach: systematic debugging, rubber-duck thinking, divide-and-conquer, or creative lateral thinking. About methodology, not the problems themselves.
anti_examples: Makes decisions by committee → use how_decision_making

labels.name: how_tech_adoption
labels.description: How they adopt new technology — early adopter vs cautious
examples: Early adopter — tries new frameworks on day one
Waits for a tool to mature before adopting it
Evaluates new tech through small proof-of-concept projects
Conservative: sticks with battle-tested tools unless there's a clear benefit
labels.classification_guidance: Describes their stance on adopting new technologies, frameworks, and tools. Ranges from bleeding-edge early adopter to conservative wait-and-see. Distinct from what tech they actually use.
anti_examples: Uses React and TypeScript → use what_tech_stack

labels.name: how_work_life_balance
labels.description: How they balance work and personal life, boundaries
examples: Strict no-work policy after 6pm
Checks email on weekends but doesn't code
Takes regular mental health days
Blends work and life — enjoys working on side projects evenings
labels.classification_guidance: Captures boundaries between work and personal life, including overtime policies, weekend availability, and personal time protection strategies.

labels.name: how_workflow
labels.description: How they organize work — task management, processes, habits
examples: Uses Todoist for personal tasks and Jira for work
Follows a strict Pomodoro technique (25/5 intervals)
Practices Agile/Scrum with 2-week sprints
Keeps a daily standup journal in Notion
labels.classification_guidance: Describes work organization: task management systems (Jira, Todoist), development processes (Agile, Kanban), personal productivity habits, and work rituals. About structure and process.
anti_examples: Most productive in the morning → use when_productivity_patterns

labels.name: what_active_projects
labels.description: Current projects they're working on
examples: Building a personal finance tracker app
Leading the migration to microservices at work
Contributing to the FastAPI open source project
Working on a machine learning side project for music recommendation
labels.classification_guidance: Lists current projects the person is actively working on, including side projects, open source contributions, and work assignments. These are temporal and change frequently.
anti_examples: Previously worked on X → use who_work_history
Wants to build a startup → use why_goals

labels.name: what_certifications
labels.description: Professional certifications, credentials, licenses
examples: AWS Solutions Architect Professional
Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA)
PMP (Project Management Professional)
Google Cloud Professional Data Engineer
labels.classification_guidance: Professional certifications, licenses, and credentials such as AWS Solutions Architect, PMP, or CPA. Distinct from academic degrees (what_education) and general skills (what_skills).
anti_examples: Good at cloud architecture → use what_skills

labels.name: what_domain_knowledge
labels.description: Subject matter expertise, specialized knowledge areas
examples: Deep expertise in payment processing and PCI compliance
Strong background in NLP and transformer architectures
Extensive knowledge of HIPAA regulations in healthcare IT
Domain expert in supply chain logistics
labels.classification_guidance: Deep domain expertise in specific fields like fintech, biotech, or real estate. Broader than skills — represents understanding of an entire domain's landscape, terminology, and best practices.

labels.name: what_education
labels.description: Educational background — degrees, schools, what they studied
examples: BS in Computer Science from MIT
Completed a full-stack bootcamp at Hack Reactor
MBA from Wharton School of Business
Self-taught programmer, no formal CS degree
labels.classification_guidance: Formal educational background including degrees, universities, bootcamps, and fields of study. Multiple entries expected for different educational milestones.

labels.name: what_interests_hobbies
labels.description: Personal interests, hobbies, leisure activities
examples: Loves hiking and trail running
Amateur photographer, mostly landscapes
Plays guitar in a local band
Board game enthusiast, especially strategy games
labels.classification_guidance: Personal interests and hobbies outside of professional work: sports, gaming, cooking, reading, music, etc. Multiple interests naturally coexist.
anti_examples: Likes using dark mode → use what_preferences

labels.name: what_preferences
labels.description: General preferences — tools, food, aesthetics, etc.
examples: Prefers dark mode in all editors and apps
Likes minimalist design aesthetics
Prefers coffee over tea, black no sugar
Favors concise documentation over verbose explanations
labels.classification_guidance: General preferences spanning tools, food, aesthetics, UI themes, and lifestyle choices. Covers the broad category of 'likes and dislikes' that don't fit neatly into other labels.

labels.name: what_publications_ip
labels.description: Published work — papers, articles, patents, IP
examples: Published a paper on distributed systems at SOSP 2024
Author of 'Building Scalable APIs' (O'Reilly, 2023)
Holds a patent on real-time data sync algorithms
Writes a popular weekly newsletter on AI engineering
labels.classification_guidance: Published works including academic papers, blog posts, patents, books, and other intellectual property. Each publication is a separate fact.
anti_examples: Writes blog posts regularly → use how_content_creation

labels.name: what_skills
labels.description: Professional skills and competencies
examples: Strong in Python and Go
Excellent at technical writing
Skilled in system design and distributed systems
Good at conflict resolution and stakeholder management
labels.classification_guidance: Professional and technical skills: programming languages, frameworks, soft skills, and competencies. Distinct from domain knowledge (broader expertise) and tech stack (specific tools in active use).
anti_examples: Uses React at work → use what_tech_stack
Expert in healthcare IT → use what_domain_knowledge

labels.name: what_tech_stack
labels.description: Technologies, programming languages, frameworks they use
examples: React + TypeScript frontend, Python FastAPI backend
AWS (EC2, Lambda, S3), Terraform for IaC
PostgreSQL and Redis for data storage
Docker and Kubernetes for container orchestration
labels.classification_guidance: The specific technologies, languages, frameworks, and tools they actively use in their current work. Distinct from skills (what they can do) — this is what they currently use.
anti_examples: Knows Java but doesn't use it → use what_skills
Uses Slack for communication → use where_digital_environments

labels.name: when_life_events
labels.description: Major life events — new job, marriage, moves, milestones
examples: Got married in June 2024
Relocated from NYC to London last month
Just had their first child
Graduated from university in 2022
labels.classification_guidance: Significant life milestones and events: marriages, births, relocations, career changes, graduations. These are discrete temporal events, not ongoing states.

labels.name: when_planning_style
labels.description: How they plan — short vs long term, structured vs flexible
examples: Plans everything in 2-week sprints
Prefers long-term roadmaps with quarterly milestones
Very spontaneous, avoids rigid schedules
Uses OKRs for quarterly and annual planning
labels.classification_guidance: Their temporal planning orientation: whether they favor short-term sprints or long-term roadmaps, structured schedules or flexible ad-hoc planning. A stable personal trait.
anti_examples: Uses Jira for task management → use how_workflow

labels.name: when_productivity_patterns
labels.description: When they're most productive, peak hours, energy patterns
examples: Most productive in early morning, 6am-10am
Creative work best in the afternoon
Post-lunch slump around 2-3pm
Peak focus on Tuesdays and Wednesdays
labels.classification_guidance: Captures peak productivity times, energy cycles, and focus patterns throughout the day or week. Multiple patterns can coexist (e.g., creative mornings, admin afternoons).
anti_examples: Prefers deep work blocks → use how_workflow

labels.name: when_response_patterns
labels.description: How quickly they respond, communication timing habits
examples: Responds to Slack within minutes during work hours
Emails usually answered within 24 hours
Slow to respond on weekends
Batches messages and replies twice a day
labels.classification_guidance: Communication timing habits: response latency, availability windows, and patterns around when they reply to messages. Multiple patterns for different channels.

labels.name: when_routines
labels.description: Daily/weekly routines and habits
examples: Morning run at 6:30am every day
Weekly team retrospective on Fridays at 3pm
Meal preps on Sundays for the week
Reads for 30 minutes before bed
labels.classification_guidance: Regular daily or weekly routines: morning rituals, workout schedules, weekly reviews, standup meetings. Multiple routines naturally coexist.
anti_examples: Works Monday to Friday → use when_work_schedule

labels.name: when_seasonal_patterns
labels.description: Seasonal variations in work, mood, availability
examples: Takes two weeks off every August for vacation
Less productive in winter months
Busy season at work is Q4 (October-December)
Academic schedule: summers are more flexible
labels.classification_guidance: Seasonal variations in availability, productivity, or mood: holiday schedules, academic calendars, fiscal year cycles, or seasonal energy patterns.
anti_examples: Takes vacation in August → use where_travel
Gets SAD in winter → use who_health

labels.name: when_timezone
labels.description: Their timezone and local time
examples: UTC-3 (Argentina Time)
Pacific Time (UTC-8)
Central European Time (UTC+1)
JST (UTC+9, Japan Standard Time)
labels.classification_guidance: The person's primary timezone. Singular because a person is in one timezone at a time. Changes when they relocate.
anti_examples: Travels to Europe often → use where_travel

labels.name: when_work_schedule
labels.description: Working hours, availability, shift patterns
examples: Works 9am to 6pm Monday through Friday
Flexible hours, usually starts around 10am
Works four 10-hour days, Fridays off
Night shift: 10pm to 6am
labels.classification_guidance: Regular working hours, shift patterns, and scheduled availability windows. Multiple schedule entries can coexist (e.g., different days have different hours).
anti_examples: Takes lunch at noon → use when_routines

labels.name: where_current_location
labels.description: Where they currently are geographically
examples: Currently in a coffee shop in Brooklyn
At a conference in Las Vegas
Working from a cabin in the mountains this week
Visiting family in Madrid
labels.classification_guidance: Current geographic location at this moment. Singular — a person can only be in one place at a time. May differ from home or work location during travel.
anti_examples: Traveling to Japan next week → use where_travel

labels.name: where_digital_environments
labels.description: Digital platforms, virtual workspaces they use
examples: Active on the company Slack workspace
Uses Notion for personal knowledge management
Contributes to several GitHub organizations
Member of three Discord communities for game dev
labels.classification_guidance: Digital platforms, virtual workspaces, and online environments they inhabit: Slack workspaces, Discord servers, GitHub organizations, Notion spaces. Multiple environments coexist.

labels.name: where_home
labels.description: Where they live, home city/country
examples: Lives in San Francisco, California
Based in Berlin, Germany
Home is in Buenos Aires, Argentina
Lives in a small town outside of Tokyo
labels.classification_guidance: Primary residence location — city, country, or region. Singular because a person has one primary home at a time. Changes supersede previous values.
anti_examples: Previously lived in London → use when_life_events

labels.name: where_travel
labels.description: Travel history, patterns, preferences, upcoming trips
examples: Planning a trip to Japan in March
Frequently travels to London for work
Visited 15 countries so far
Prefers off-the-beaten-path destinations
labels.classification_guidance: Travel history, upcoming trips, travel preferences, and frequently visited destinations. Multiple travel facts naturally coexist.

labels.name: where_work
labels.description: Where they work — office location, company address
examples: Google campus in Mountain View, CA
WeWork co-working space in downtown Manhattan
Remote — company HQ is in Austin, TX
Office in Shoreditch, London
labels.classification_guidance: Primary work location — office address, city, or campus. Singular because a person typically has one primary work location. For remote workers, this may be the company HQ or 'remote'.

labels.name: where_work_environment
labels.description: Work setup — remote, hybrid, office, home office
examples: Fully remote, works from home
Hybrid — 3 days in office, 2 remote
In-office five days a week
Digital nomad, works from co-working spaces
labels.classification_guidance: The type of work environment: fully remote, hybrid, in-office, co-working space, or home office setup. Singular as it represents the current primary arrangement.
anti_examples: Office is in San Francisco → use where_work
Has a standing desk → use what_preferences

labels.name: who_age
labels.description: Their age, date of birth, generation
examples: Born on March 15, 1990
32 years old
Millennial (born in 1988)
In their late twenties
labels.classification_guidance: Age, date of birth, or generational cohort (Gen Z, Millennial, etc.). Singular — a person has one age/DOB. New values supersede old ones.

labels.name: who_communication_style
labels.description: Their communication tone — formal, casual, direct, verbose
examples: Very direct and to-the-point
Formal in writing, casual in person
Uses lots of emojis and informal language
Diplomatic and avoids confrontation
labels.classification_guidance: Personal communication tone and style: formal vs casual, direct vs diplomatic, verbose vs terse. A personality-adjacent trait distinct from communication channel preferences (how_communication).

labels.name: who_communities
labels.description: Groups, organizations, communities they belong to
examples: Active member of the Python Discord server
Part of the local running club
Member of ACM and IEEE
Volunteer at the neighborhood food bank
labels.classification_guidance: Professional and personal communities, organizations, clubs, and groups the person belongs to. Multiple memberships naturally coexist.

labels.name: who_contact_info
labels.description: Email, phone, contact details
examples: alex@example.com (personal email)
Telegram: @alexj
alex.johnson@company.com (work email)
labels.classification_guidance: Contact information: email addresses, phone numbers, messaging handles. Multiple contact methods naturally coexist.

labels.name: who_employment_status
labels.description: Employed, freelance, unemployed, retired, student
examples: Full-time employed
Freelance consultant
Between jobs, actively looking
Part-time while finishing PhD
labels.classification_guidance: Current employment status: employed full-time, part-time, freelance, self-employed, unemployed, retired, or student. Singular — one primary status at a time.
anti_examples: Works as a software engineer → use who_role

labels.name: who_family
labels.description: Family situation — spouse, children, dependents
examples: Married with two children (ages 5 and 8)
Single, lives with a roommate
Has a partner named Sarah
Taking care of elderly parents
labels.classification_guidance: Family situation including spouse/partner, children, parents, siblings, and dependents. Multiple family facts coexist (e.g., has a wife AND two kids).
anti_examples: Close friend named Bob → use who_relationships
Got married last year → use when_life_events

labels.name: who_finances
labels.description: Financial situation, income level, budget concerns
examples: Comfortable salary, saving for a house
Freelance income varies month to month
Has student loan debt of about $40K
Recently started investing in index funds
labels.classification_guidance: Financial situation, income range, budget constraints, savings goals, and financial concerns. Multiple financial facts can coexist (income, debt, savings goals).
anti_examples: Wants to save for a house → use why_goals

labels.name: who_gender
labels.description: Gender identity, pronouns
examples: Male, he/him
Non-binary, they/them
Female, she/her
Prefers not to disclose
labels.classification_guidance: Gender identity and preferred pronouns. Singular — a person has one gender identity. Updates supersede previous values.

labels.name: who_health
labels.description: Health status, conditions, wellness, fitness
examples: Vegetarian for ethical reasons
Manages mild asthma with an inhaler
Runs 5K three times a week
Lactose intolerant
labels.classification_guidance: Health-related information: medical conditions, fitness level, wellness practices, dietary restrictions, and health goals. Multiple health facts coexist.

labels.name: who_industry
labels.description: What industry/sector they work in
examples: Fintech / financial services
Healthcare and biotech
E-commerce and retail
Education technology
labels.classification_guidance: The industry or sector they work in: fintech, healthcare, education, e-commerce, etc. Can have multiple if they work across industries.
anti_examples: Works as a PM → use who_role

labels.name: who_languages
labels.description: Languages they speak, fluency levels
examples: Native English speaker
Fluent in Spanish and Portuguese
Learning Japanese (beginner level)
Bilingual: French and Arabic
labels.classification_guidance: Spoken and written languages with fluency levels. Multiple languages naturally coexist (e.g., native English, conversational Spanish).

labels.name: who_name
labels.description: Their name — first, last, preferred, display name
examples: Alex Johnson
Dr. Maria Garcia
Goes by Mike (Michael Thompson)
张伟 (Wei Zhang)
labels.classification_guidance: The person's name: first name, last name, preferred name, or display name. Singular — new name information supersedes old (e.g., name change, correction).
anti_examples: Goes by @alex on Twitter → use who_social_presence

labels.name: who_nationality_ethnicity
labels.description: Nationality, ethnicity, cultural background
examples: Argentine, born and raised in Buenos Aires
Dual citizenship: US and Italian
Korean-American, second generation
British with South Asian heritage
labels.classification_guidance: Nationality, ethnicity, and cultural background. Can be plural for dual citizenship or mixed heritage.

labels.name: who_personality
labels.description: Personality type, traits — MBTI, Big Five, temperament
examples: INTJ personality type
Introverted but warm in small groups
High conscientiousness, moderate openness (Big Five)
Analytical and detail-oriented temperament
labels.classification_guidance: Personality traits, temperament, and type indicators like MBTI (INTJ), Big Five scores, or general descriptors (introverted, analytical). Singular as it represents a holistic self-assessment.

labels.name: who_relationships
labels.description: Professional and personal relationships, who they work with
examples: Works closely with Jake on the backend team
Mentored by Dr. Chen at university
Best friends with Lisa since college
Regular collaborator with the DevOps team
labels.classification_guidance: Professional and personal relationships: colleagues, mentors, friends, collaborators. Multiple relationships naturally coexist.
anti_examples: Member of Python community → use who_communities

labels.name: who_role
labels.description: Job role, title, position, responsibilities
examples: Senior Software Engineer at Google
Product Manager, Growth Team
CTO and co-founder of a startup
Freelance UX Designer
labels.classification_guidance: Current job role, title, and primary responsibilities. Singular — represents the current primary role. Changes when they switch jobs.
anti_examples: Previously was a junior dev → use who_work_history

labels.name: who_seniority
labels.description: Seniority level — junior, mid, senior, lead, executive
examples: Senior level (IC5)
Engineering Lead
Mid-level, about 4 years of experience
VP of Engineering
labels.classification_guidance: Current seniority level in their career: junior, mid-level, senior, lead, staff, principal, director, VP, or executive. Singular — one level at a time.
anti_examples: Works as a software engineer → use who_role

labels.name: who_social_presence
labels.description: Social media profiles, online presence, followers
examples: Twitter/X: @alexdev with 5K followers
GitHub: github.com/alexj — active open source contributor
Personal blog at alexjohnson.dev
LinkedIn profile with 2K connections
labels.classification_guidance: Social media profiles, online presence, follower counts, and personal websites. Multiple profiles across platforms coexist.
anti_examples: Member of DevOps community → use who_communities

labels.name: who_work_history
labels.description: Past jobs, career path, employment history
examples: Previously worked at Amazon as a SDE for 3 years
Started career as a junior designer at a small agency
Transitioned from marketing to software engineering in 2020
Co-founded a startup in 2018 that was acquired in 2021
labels.classification_guidance: Employment history, past roles, career trajectory, and previous companies. Multiple entries naturally coexist as career milestones accumulate.
anti_examples: Currently a PM at Google → use who_role
Started a new job → use when_life_events

labels.name: why_aspirations
labels.description: Long-term dreams, what they aspire to become
examples: Wants to become a CTO at a mid-size company
Dreams of writing a bestselling technical book
Aspires to build a startup that makes education accessible
Hopes to retire early and travel the world
labels.classification_guidance: Long-term dreams and aspirations: what they want to become, where they see themselves in 5-10 years, life ambitions. More future-oriented and abstract than concrete goals.
anti_examples: Wants to finish the project by Friday → use why_goals

labels.name: why_fears
labels.description: Professional and personal fears, anxieties, worries
examples: Imposter syndrome in senior-level meetings
Worried about job stability in the current market
Anxious about public speaking
Fear of making the wrong career decision
labels.classification_guidance: Professional and personal fears, anxieties, and worries: fear of failure, job loss, imposter syndrome, health concerns. Multiple fears coexist.
anti_examples: Frustrated with slow CI → use why_pain_points

labels.name: why_goals
labels.description: Current goals — career, personal, project-level
examples: Get promoted to Senior Engineer this year
Ship the v2 of the product by end of Q1
Learn Rust and build a side project with it
Run a half marathon in under 2 hours
labels.classification_guidance: Current concrete goals: career milestones, project deliverables, personal targets, learning objectives. More actionable and near-term than aspirations.
anti_examples: Dreams of starting a company → use why_aspirations
Focuses on family first → use why_priorities

labels.name: why_pain_points
labels.description: Frustrations, challenges, things that bother them
examples: Frustrated with slow CI/CD pipeline at work
Too many meetings killing deep work time
Struggling with the legacy codebase
Annoyed by constant context switching between projects
labels.classification_guidance: Current frustrations, challenges, and pain points in work or life. Things that bother them or slow them down. Multiple pain points coexist.
anti_examples: Afraid of public speaking → use why_fears

labels.name: why_priorities
labels.description: What they prioritize, what matters most right now
examples: Family comes first, work second
Currently prioritizing career growth over compensation
Health and fitness are top priority this quarter
Shipping the MVP is the #1 focus right now
labels.classification_guidance: Current priorities and what matters most to them right now. What they choose to focus on when trade-offs are needed. Multiple priorities can coexist in ranked order.
anti_examples: Goal is to ship v2 → use why_goals

labels.name: why_values_motivations
labels.description: Core values, what motivates and drives them
examples: Values autonomy and independence above all
Motivated by building things that help people
Believes strongly in open source and knowledge sharing
Driven by craftsmanship — quality over speed
labels.classification_guidance: Core personal and professional values, intrinsic motivations, and driving principles: autonomy, impact, craftsmanship, fairness. Deep and relatively stable traits.
